issues.description: The try/except wrapping the psutil affinity check was removed, so on platforms where psutil.Process.cpu_affinity() raises (e.g., macOS raises NotImplementedError, or AccessDenied errors elsewhere), cpu_count() will now raise instead of falling back gracefully as before.
Using bare `assert count` for validating count in production code is risky since assertions can be stripped with python -O, silently skipping this sanity check.
The psutil affinity test is skipped on macOS, meaning the removed exception handling regression is not exercised by CI on the very platform most likely to trigger it.
New import of LINUX from dask._compatibility assumes this module/constant exists and is stable API, but its definition isn't shown in the diff.

Comment claims psutil affinity check applies regardless of Python version because os.process_cpu_count() doesn't reflect psutil-set affinity on Windows, but this isn't verified for Linux/macOS in 3.13+, potentially causing redundant or incorrect min() operations across platforms.

item_8.evidence: Comments explain rationale for version checks and platform differences, aiding understanding without needing external context.

item_9.evidence: Removal of exception handling around psutil affinity check introduces a plausible crash on macOS or restricted environments.

item_10.evidence: Given the regression risk from removed exception handling, a careful reviewer would want this fixed before merging.

issues.description: Removed the try/except around psutil.Process()/cpu_affinity() calls, so exceptions (e.g. permission errors, unsupported platforms, race conditions) will now propagate and crash cpu_count() instead of being silently ignored as before.

The new assert affinity will raise an AssertionError if psutil returns an empty list (previously handled by checking affinity_count > 0), which is a plausible edge case that will now crash instead of falling back.

assert count immediately after `os.cpu_count() or 1` seems redundant since count can never be falsy at that point, but it doesn't guard against other unexpected falsy values from process_cpu_count/sched_getaffinity paths consistently.
Top-level `psutil = pytest.importorskip("psutil")` was removed, so tests not explicitly importing psutil now run even without it installed, potentially changing test coverage/skip behavior silently.
New import `from dask._compatibility import LINUX` assumes this module/attribute exists; if not previously present, this could introduce an import error not visible in the diff.

item_1.evidence: try/except Exception: pass around psutil affinity check was removed, so exceptions previously swallowed will now propagate from cpu_count()

item_2.evidence: New asserts (assert count, assert affinity) can raise AssertionError on edge cases like empty affinity lists that were previously handled gracefully

item_3.evidence: Test file substantially rewritten with new tests for psutil affinity, taskset, cpu_count arg, and platform-specific skips

item_4.evidence: PR focuses solely on improving CPU affinity detection logic in system.py and corresponding tests

item_5.evidence: No security-sensitive code paths introduced; changes affect CPU count computation only

item_6.evidence: No performance-relevant changes such as loops or heavy computation added; only minor extra checks

item_7.evidence: Uses similar style with sys.version_info checks and hasattr guards consistent with existing codebase conventions

item_8.evidence: Code is reasonably documented with comments explaining Python version behavior and platform differences

item_9.evidence: Removal of exception handling around psutil calls could cause crashes in production environments where errors were previously silently ignored

item_10.evidence: Despite good test coverage, the loss of exception handling around psutil.Process() calls is a regression risk that warrants changes before merge

parsed.justification: Solid, well-tested improvement to CPU affinity detection, but removing the try/except around psutil calls and adding asserts risks converting previously silent failures into crashes.
